# Registering on PROSPERO and risk of bias {#sec-prospero}



Chapter 2 left us with a review we believe is viable: enough studies, enough
dose levels, a reference in each, and enough printed per level to reconstruct
the covariance. We also left it with a search strategy and an extraction
template. What we do not yet have is a public record of what we intend to do
with them.

This chapter writes that record, in three blocks, the same three the class
follows. The first covers the **PROSPERO basics**: when to register, and how to
write a protocol that still has room to move. The second goes to the **main
differences**, the numbered PROSPERO questions where a dose-response review
says something a standard review never has to say: 1.5, 2.1 to 2.4, 8.1 and,
above all, 9.1. The third chooses the **risk of bias** tool, which follows the
design of each study rather than the design of the review.

It is not a tour of the whole form. Most of the form is the same form every
systematic review fills in, and there are better places to learn it than a book
about one design. Each field below is named as PROSPERO words it on screen,
with its number beside it, so the chapter can be read with the form open.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The worked example**

Every draft in this chapter answers one question: habitual alcohol intake, in
grams of ethanol per day, against cardiovascular disease. It is the question
behind `alcohol_cvd`, which ships with **{easyDR}** and holds six exposure
contrasts from four studies, reported as an effect with confidence limits plus
the cases and totals per category.

The risk of bias block also uses `aripiprazole`, the five randomised,
fixed-dose trials of Crippa and Orsini [-@crippa2016], because a set of trials
lands on a different tool than a set of observational studies. This chapter
fits nothing, so no code is shown in it.
:::

## PROSPERO basics

### Protocol registration

Prospective registration on PROSPERO means lodging the protocol with the Centre
for Reviews and Dissemination at York before the review has produced any
results, and accepting that the record is public and versioned from then on.
Anybody can read what we said we would do, and compare it with what we did.
Three habits keep a protocol honest from the day we submit it.

#### Register before data extraction

The timing rule is more generous than it sounds. **You can still register once
the inclusion and exclusion criteria are locked, right up to the point you
start pulling data.** Searching may be done. Screening may be done. Deciding
which studies meet the criteria may be done. What may not be done is
extracting the numbers, because the numbers are what the analysis plan is
about, and a plan written after seeing them is not a plan.

Why insist on this harder in a dose-response review than in an ordinary one?
Because this design has more defensible analyses than any other in the
meta-analytic family. Let us count the choices a protocol has to commit to.


::: {#tbl-shapes-count .cell tbl-cap='The modelling choices a dose-response protocol has to commit to, with the defensible options in each.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Choice                       |Options                                                        |
|:----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
|Functional form              |linear, log, quadratic, cubic, rcs, fp, emax, hyperbolic_emax  |
|Knot placement, for a spline |three knots, placed at any of five common percentiles          |
|Pooling stage                |two-stage or one-stage                                         |
|Reference level              |study reference, or re-expressed to a common one               |
|Dose assigned to a category  |median or mean, midpoint, or a stated rule for open categories |


:::
:::


We see that five decisions are open before a single number is read, and that
none of them has one right answer. Multiply the options together and the same
extraction sheet supports well over a hundred analyses, each of which would
survive peer review on its own. Some of them will show a rising curve, some a
plateau, some a J shape. Choosing among them after seeing all of them is the
practice known as **researcher degrees of freedom**, and in this design the
freedom is unusually wide.

This is why `easydr()` has no default shape. Asking for a fit without naming
`shape` produces an error rather than a straight line, and the error lists what
may be written instead. The package refuses the choice because the choice is a
claim about biology, and the place for it is the protocol, with a reason beside
it.

#### Talk in the future

**Every section describes what will be done, not what has already been done.**
We will search, we will screen, we will extract, we will fit. This is not a
stylistic convention. The tense is the evidence of when the document was
written, and a protocol in the past tense is a report wearing a protocol's
clothes.

#### Avoid setting things in stone

That leaves a genuine tension, and it is the one authors get wrong most often. A
protocol has to commit, or it offers no protection. Yet we cannot honestly
commit to a shape we have not seen data for, or to a test of non-linearity
whose result we do not know. Write it too tightly and we will break our own
protocol in month four. Write it too loosely and we have registered nothing.

The way out is **conditional language**: if this subgroup shows up, we will do
X; if that effect appears, we will do Y. We commit to the **rule** rather than
to the **result**. A conditional plan names three things: the trigger, the
action that follows it, and what gets reported either way.

Let us see the difference on one decision, the functional form.

> *We will fit the most appropriate dose-response model.*

That is a blank cheque. "Appropriate" is decided later, by us, using
information we do not have yet, and no reader can tell whether we kept the
promise, because the promise cannot be broken.

> *A restricted cubic spline with three knots at the 10th, 50th and 90th
> percentiles of the pooled intake distribution is planned. It will be compared
> with the linear model by the Wald test for non-linearity. If other knot
> placements change the shape, this will be reported as a knot sensitivity.*

That is a plan. The trigger is a named test, the action follows from it, and
the reader learns what happens whichever way the test falls.

::: {.callout-important}
**The test of a contingency**

Hand your protocol and your extraction sheet to a stranger. If that person
would arrive at the same primary model you did, you wrote a plan. If the person
would have to ask you what you meant, you wrote a preference.
:::

## PROSPERO: main differences

Now to the form itself. The PROSPERO record has twelve sections and roughly
forty numbered questions, and most of them are filled in exactly as they would
be for any review. Let us go only to the ones this design forces us to word
differently.


::: {#tbl-fields .cell tbl-cap='The numbered PROSPERO questions a dose-response review answers differently, and what changes in each.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Question                           |Changes                                                       |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
|1.5 Review objectives              |Asks for the shape of the association, not whether one exists |
|2.1 Population                     |Says which part of the intake range the population covers     |
|2.2 Intervention(s) or exposure(s) |Names one unit, the conversion rule and one dose per category |
|2.3 Comparator(s) or control(s)    |A level rather than a group: each study's own reference       |
|2.4 Study design                   |Names each design; the three-level rule stays out of it       |
|8.1 Main outcomes                  |One outcome per curve, with the effect measure beside it      |
|9.1 Strategy for data synthesis    |The covariance, the pooling stage, the shapes, the knots      |


:::
:::


We see that the changes cluster in Section 2, which defines eligibility, and in
Section 9, which defines the analysis. Searching, Section 6, changed too, but
we settled that in Chapter 2 when we agreed to keep the outcome out of the
search string.

Each field below shows the draft answer as it would be typed into the box,
followed by what each numbered phrase of the draft does. The numbers match the
phrases of the draft, in order.

### 1.5 Review objectives

**Question 1.5**, 10 to 200 words, required.

A standard meta-analysis asks whether an exposure is associated with an
outcome. Our question is different in kind. We ask how the association
**behaves** as the dose rises: whether it climbs in a straight line, flattens
after some intake, reverses, or shows no trend at all. A protocol whose
question is "is alcohol associated with cardiovascular disease" has registered
the wrong review, and every field downstream inherits the error.

> *To characterize the shape of the dose-response relationship (1) between
> habitual alcohol intake, in grams of ethanol per day, (2) and the risk of
> cardiovascular disease (3) in general adult populations. (4)*

1. **The shape of the association.** The review asks about a curve, not a yes
   or no.
2. **Exposure and its unit.** The dose is a quantity, and the unit is fixed
   here, once.
3. **One outcome.** One curve belongs to one outcome.
4. **Target population.** Whom the curve describes.

### 2.1 Population

**Question 2.1**, an inclusion box and an exclusion box.

This question changes least, and it changes once. What a dose-response review
adds is the **part of the intake range the population covers**, because a
population none of whose members reach a high dose cannot inform the upper
half of the curve, however many of them there are.

> *Inclusion: Adults aged 18 or over, drawn from general populations. (1)
> Populations limited to light drinkers will be included and flagged, since
> they cover only the lower end of the intake range. (2)*
>
> *Exclusion: Populations selected for an existing cardiovascular
> diagnosis. (3)*

1. **Who the participants are.**
2. **Part of the intake range.** A cohort of light drinkers is a legitimate
   study of alcohol. It cannot tell us what happens at 60 grams a day, and
   flagging it now means a band that opens out at the right-hand edge of the
   figure will not surprise us later.
3. **Outcome already present.** A population selected for the outcome cannot
   tell us how the risk of that outcome changes with intake.

### 2.2 Intervention(s) or exposure(s)

**Question 2.2**, PICO tags (Alcoholic Drink, Ethanol) and two boxes.

This is the question with no counterpart in a standard review, and it is where
most of the later pain is prevented.

> *Inclusion: Habitual alcohol intake recorded as a quantity and expressed as
> grams of ethanol per day. (1) Where a study reports intake in drinks or in
> another unit, we will convert using the ethanol content stated by that study,
> or 12 grams per standard drink where none is stated. (2) Each exposure
> category will be assigned the median or mean intake reported by the authors;
> where only the range is reported, its midpoint. An open-ended lowest category
> will start at zero, and an open-ended highest category will be given the same
> width as the category below it before its midpoint is taken. (3)*
>
> *Exclusion: Intake recorded only as ever or never drinking, or as a drinking
> pattern with no quantity attached. (4)*

1. **One unit for every study.** The curve has one horizontal axis, so every
   study has to land on it.
2. **Converted at extraction.** The conversion rule is written before we see
   which rule makes the curve look better.
3. **One dose per category.** Published papers report bands rather than doses,
   and the model needs one number per band. A cohort reporting "1 to 14
   grams", "15 to 29" and "30 or more" has an open highest category; with this
   rule it becomes 30 to 45, and its dose is 37.5. Any rule will do, as long
   as it is written down first.
4. **Intake without a quantity.** "Ever drinker" has no position on the dose
   axis.

### 2.3 Comparator(s) or control(s)

**Question 2.3**, three radio buttons, a PICO tag (Abstinence) and two boxes.

In an ordinary review the comparator is a **group**. In ours it is a **level**,
and each study supplies its own.

> *The comparator is a level of intake rather than a separate group. (1) Each
> study contributes its own reference category, usually its lowest intake,
> whose dose is assigned like any other category: the reported median or mean,
> otherwise the midpoint, starting at zero when the range is open. Estimates
> are kept against it in the primary analysis. (2) Where the references differ
> widely, estimates will also be re-expressed against a common reference by the
> method of Hamling and colleagues, as a sensitivity analysis. (3)*

1. **The comparator is a level.** The reference is a point on the same dose
   axis, not a different treatment.
2. **Each study's own reference.** The primary analysis keeps every estimate
   against the category the study itself compared with.
3. **Common reference as sensitivity analysis.** Studies disagree about what
   the reference should be, and the estimates can be re-expressed against a
   common one [@hamling2008]. Saying so here protects us: a reader who sees
   "each study's own reference" and then meets a common reference in the
   results has caught us changing the comparator after the fact.

### 2.4 Study design

**Question 2.4**, a checkbox for randomised and non-randomised studies, then an
inclusion box (250 words) and an exclusion box (150 words).

The field guide gives one instruction that saves trouble later: never write
"observational studies" as a design. Name them. The designs named here also
decide which risk of bias tools the review needs, as we will see in the last
block.

> *Inclusion: Prospective cohort, retrospective cohort, nested case-control and
> case-control studies. (1)*
>
> *Exclusion: Cross-sectional studies, case reports, case series, narrative
> reviews, and conference abstracts without a full report. (2)*

1. **Designs named one by one.**
2. **Designs excluded.** Each one named, so nobody has to guess what
   "observational" meant.

::: {.callout-important}
**The three-level rule is a pooling rule, not an eligibility criterion**

It is tempting to write Chapter 2's viability rule into 2.4, so that a study
reporting two exposure levels is simply ineligible. The rule belongs in **9.1
Strategy for data synthesis**, where it decides which analysis a study enters
rather than whether the study exists. Some protocols list it under eligibility
instead [@garcia2023]. Either way, say what happens to studies with fewer
levels.
:::

### 8.1 Main outcomes

**Question 8.1**, 5 to 250 words, required.

PROSPERO asks for the outcome definition, the acceptable measurement
instruments, the timepoints, and **the effect measure to be used in
synthesis**. That last item is easy to skip, and it is the one that has to
agree with 9.1.

> *Incident cardiovascular disease, fatal or non-fatal, (1) as defined by each
> study against ICD codes or an adjudicated endpoint, (2) at the longest
> follow-up reported. (3) The effect measure is the relative risk at each level
> of intake against the reference, taking risk ratios, hazard ratios and odds
> ratios as reported. (4)*

1. **Primary outcome.** Named now, before we discover which outcome has the
   most interesting shape.
2. **How it is measured.**
3. **Timepoint.** One per study, chosen by a rule rather than by the result.
4. **Effect measure.** Each level of intake against the study's reference,
   which is what the model pools.

### 9.1 Strategy for data synthesis

**Question 9.1**, 30 to 500 words, required, after a radio asking whether
formal synthesis is planned.

Here is the box that carries the chapter, and the hardest one in the form. The
synthesis plan is the core difference between this record and the record of a
standard review, so the draft runs long, and we read it in two parts. A box
reading "a random effects meta-analysis will be performed and heterogeneity
assessed with $I^2$" describes no review in particular, and a record carrying it
gets flagged as a template.

> *Within-study covariances will be reconstructed by the method of Greenland and
> Longnecker, using the approximation appropriate to each study's design. (1)
> Studies will be pooled by two-stage random-effects meta-analysis with
> restricted maximum likelihood. Studies reporting fewer than three exposure
> levels cannot enter the two-stage spline; they will be named, and a one-stage
> model including every study will be run as a sensitivity analysis. (2) A
> restricted cubic spline model with three knots at the 10th, 50th and 90th
> percentiles of the pooled intake distribution is planned. It will be compared
> with the linear model by the Wald test for non-linearity, and with Emax and
> fractional polynomial models by AIC and BIC; its fit will be checked with the
> deviance test, R-squared and adjusted R-squared. If other knot placements
> change the shape, this will be reported as a knot sensitivity. (3) The pooled
> curve will be shown with its 95% confidence band and read only within the
> range of intake observed in the included studies. (4)*

1. **Within-study covariance.** Estimates within a study share a reference
   group, so they are correlated, and the correlation is reconstructed by the
   method of Greenland and Longnecker [-@greenland1992], with the approximation
   chosen by each study's design [@orsini2006]. easyDR calls dosresmeta, which
   does this reconstruction.
2. **Pooling stage and fallback.** Two-stage estimation fits a trend inside
   each study and then pools the trends [@orsini2012]. One-stage estimation
   fits every study inside a single mixed model [@crippa2019]. The choice reads
   as a default and its fallback:
   - **Default.** Pool by two stages. Every study with three or more exposure
     levels (the reference and two doses) fits its own curve.
   - **When the default fails.** If a study reports only two levels, it cannot
     fit a spline of its own, so it is named and kept for a one-stage
     sensitivity analysis that includes every study. If the review is viable
     only through the one-stage model, it is not viable.
3. **Spline and model comparison.** The reason for the primary shape comes from
   the exposure rather than from the data: whether a plateau or a threshold is
   plausible, and what comparable reviews fitted. For alcohol and
   cardiovascular disease the literature is split between a steady rise and a
   J shape, so a spline is primary and the linear model sits beside it. The
   knots are named in advance. If the shape we report depends on which
   placement we chose, the conclusion is that the shape is not established,
   and the protocol commits us to saying so.
4. **Curve read within the observed range.** The most common over-reach in this
   literature is reading a curve beyond the doses the studies observed. It
   belongs in the analysis plan, not in a tactful discussion paragraph later.

### 9.1 Strategy for data synthesis (continued)

The second half of the box covers what happens to the studies the model cannot
take, and how far we trust the curve.

> *Studies with two exposure levels will enter the one-stage sensitivity
> analysis; effects without counts will enter with their confidence
> intervals. (1) Heterogeneity will be reported with the Q test and the I²
> statistic, and shown by plotting the study-specific curves of the two-stage
> analysis. (2) Egger's regression will be used if at least ten studies enter
> the model; with fewer, the funnel plot will be inspected and no test
> claimed. (3) Each study will be omitted in turn, and any study whose omission
> moves the pooled curve will be named. (4) Subgroup analyses by study design
> are planned, with a test for subgroup interaction from a meta-regression;
> with fewer than ten studies per characteristic, a non-significant test will
> not be read as agreement. Analyses will be run in R with easyDR and
> dosresmeta. (5)*

1. **Studies with two levels.** They are not dropped from the review. They
   enter the one-stage model, and the protocol says so here, where we promised
   in 2.4 to put the rule.
2. **Heterogeneity.** Here it lives in the coefficients of a curve rather than
   in one effect, so a lone $I^2$ describes the pooled trend and not the
   agreement between shapes. The study-specific curves let the reader see the
   disagreement directly.
3. **Small-study effects.**
   - **Default.** Inspect the funnel plot.
   - **When the default fails.** If ten or more studies enter the model, add
     Egger's regression test [@egger1997]. Below ten, the test has very little
     power [@sterne2011], and a null result from eight studies means almost
     nothing, so no test is claimed.
4. **Leave-one-out.** A pooled curve that rests on one cohort is a finding,
   not an inconvenience, so the study is named.
5. **Subgroups and software.** By study design, because design decides how
   each study's covariance is approximated. The software is named, because a
   spline basis and a knot placement are implementation details as much as
   statistical ones: _R_, with **{easyDR}** calling **{dosresmeta}**
   [@dosresmeta].

## Risk of bias

### Choosing the right tool

There is no risk of bias tool for dose-response meta-analysis, and we should
be glad of it. The thing being rated is a study, and what a study needs rated
depends on how it was conducted, not on what we intend to do with it
afterwards. **The tool follows the design of the study being rated**, as the
MAA course teaches.


::: {#tbl-rob .cell tbl-cap='The risk of bias tool follows the design of the study being rated.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Design                                  |Tool                                   |Where                                 |
|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
|Randomised trial                        |RoB 2                                  |riskofbias.info/welcome/rob-2-0-tool  |
|Non-randomised study of an intervention |ROBINS-I                               |riskofbias.info/welcome/robins-i-v2   |
|Cohort study of an exposure             |ROBINS-E                               |riskofbias.info/welcome/robins-e-tool |
|Single-arm study or case series         |JBI Checklist for Case Series          |jbi.global/critical-appraisal-tools   |
|Case-control study                      |JBI Checklist for Case Control Studies |jbi.global/critical-appraisal-tools   |


:::
:::


One detail of the PROSPERO screen is worth knowing before it is reached. **A
JBI tick has to name its own checklist.** JBI publishes a checklist per design,
and ticking "JBI tools" without naming the checklist leaves the record
ambiguous, so the table above names each one.

Dose-response reviews mix designs more often than other reviews do, because the
exposure is a quantity, and quantities get measured in whatever study happens
to record them. Our two examples show it. Let us look at the binary one.


::: {#tbl-designs .cell tbl-cap='The design of each study in the binary example, as the extraction sheet recorded it.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Study             |Design               |
|:-----------------|:--------------------|
|Bianchi           |case-control         |
|Bobak             |case-control         |
|Malarcher-wine    |case-control         |
|Malarcher-beer    |case-control         |
|Vliegenthart-wine |cumulative incidence |
|Vliegenthart-beer |cumulative incidence |


:::
:::


We see that four of the six contrasts come from case-control studies and two
from studies reporting cumulative incidence, which are cohorts of an exposure.
The cohorts would be rated with **ROBINS-E** and the case-control studies with
the **JBI Checklist for Case Control Studies**. The five aripiprazole studies,
by contrast, are randomised, fixed-dose trials, so a single tool serves for all
of them, and it is **RoB 2**.

**When cohort and case-control studies are pooled, rate them with one tool, or
report the two ratings separately.** Ratings from two different tools are not
on one scale, so they are never counted into a single tally of low-risk
studies.

PROSPERO also asks how the rating will be done, and the answer is the ordinary
one: independently by two reviewers, disagreements resolved by discussion and
by a third reviewer where needed.

#### The domain that matters most here

Among the domains any of these tools asks about, one carries more weight in a
dose-response review than anywhere else: **exposure measurement**.

In a review of one high-against-low contrast, error in measuring the exposure
blurs the contrast and widens the interval. In a dose-response review it does
something worse. Error in the dose that is the same for cases and non-cases
does not scatter the curve evenly: it pulls high doses down and low doses up,
which flattens the trend toward the null. A review built on studies that
measured intake with a single food-frequency questionnaire will tend to find a
shallower curve than the truth, and a shallow curve is easy to read as
reassuring.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Reporting it: the risk of bias field**

> *Cohort studies of an exposure will be assessed with ROBINS-E, and
> case-control studies with the JBI Checklist for Case Control Studies.
> Randomised trials, if any are included, will be assessed with RoB 2. Two
> reviewers will rate each study independently, with disagreements resolved by
> discussion and by a third reviewer where needed. Ratings from different tools
> will be reported separately and will not be combined into one count.*
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Test your knowledge!**

1. A team has completed its search, screened titles and abstracts, and agreed a
   final list of 14 included studies. They have not opened a spreadsheet. Is it
   too late to register on PROSPERO, and why?
2. A cohort reports alcohol intake as 0, 1 to 14, 15 to 29, and 30 or more
   grams per day. Which numbered PROSPERO question settles the dose of each
   category, and what dose does the open highest category get under this
   chapter's rule?
3. A team writes "studies must report at least three exposure categories" into
   2.4 Study design. Where does the requirement belong, and what happens there
   to a study with two levels?
4. A review includes four randomised dose-finding trials and seven cohorts.
   Which tools does the record name, and how are their ratings reported?

Answers to these questions are listed in Appendix A.
:::

## Summary

- Registration happens before data extraction begins. Searching and screening
  may already be complete, because the analysis plan is about numbers we have
  not yet read.

- A protocol is written in the future tense, and it commits to rules rather
  than to results, in conditional language: if this happens, we will do that.

- A dose-response review has more defensible analyses than any other design,
  since the functional form, the knots, the pooling stage, the reference level
  and the dose assigned to each category are all genuine choices. The protocol
  stops those choices from being made by the result.

- The questions that change are 1.5, 2.1 to 2.4, 8.1 and 9.1. They ask for the
  shape rather than the existence of an association, the part of the intake
  range covered, one unit and one dose per category, a level as comparator,
  designs named one by one, the effect measure, and everything about the model.

- The three-level rule is a pooling rule. It sits in 9.1: two-stage pooling is
  primary, and studies with two levels enter a one-stage sensitivity analysis.

- The risk of bias tool follows the design of the study: RoB 2, ROBINS-I,
  ROBINS-E, or the JBI checklist named individually. Ratings from different
  tools are reported separately.

- Exposure measurement is the domain that matters most here, because error in
  the dose flattens the curve toward the null.
